name: docker
tasks: which compose file started a container
save an image for an air-gapped server

examples.does: Running containers: name, image, status and ports
Every container, stopped ones too (Exited (1) means it failed)
The last 100 log lines of one container
The containers of the compose project in this folder
The last 100 log lines of one compose service
The images on this server, with their size
Follow a container's log, from 10 minutes back (Ctrl+C stops)
CPU, memory and network use of each running container, once
Why a container stopped: state, exit code, killed for memory, restart count
A shell inside a running container (exit leaves it)
Which server ports a container publishes
Disk used by images, containers, volumes and build cache
Start or update the compose project in this folder, in the background
Restart one service's containers
Which compose file started a container
Which server folders a container uses
The containers of one compose project
The compose file as Docker reads it, every variable filled in
Stop and remove the project's containers and networks (volumes stay)
Save an image to a file, to carry to an air-gapped server
Load an image from a saved file
Delete dangling images (untagged leftovers of builds)

pitfalls: docker compose config prints every value from .env, passwords included: don't paste its output.
On an air-gapped server a deleted image can't be pulled again: docker save it first.
docker logs shows only what the app writes to its output; an app that logs to a file needs docker exec to read it.
docker compose commands act on the project in the current folder (or the one given with -f).

name: kubectl
summary: Kubernetes: pods, deployments, nodes and logs

examples.does: Which cluster and login kubectl uses now
Every cluster login in your kubeconfig; * marks the current one
The cluster's nodes: Ready or not, version, IP addresses
Every pod in every namespace, with status and restarts
The pods of one namespace, with node and pod IP
One pod in detail; Events at the bottom say why it isn't running
A pod's log
The log of the run before the last restart (for CrashLoopBackOff)
Follow the log of one of a deployment's pods (Ctrl+C stops)
Recent events, newest last: failed pulls, scheduling, kills
CPU and memory per pod (needs metrics-server in the cluster)
The deployments, services and ingresses of a namespace
Wait for a rollout and say whether it finished
What your login may do in a namespace
A shell inside a pod's container (exit leaves it)
Switch kubectl to another cluster login
Pods that aren't Running (finished jobs show as Succeeded)
Every pod with its UID (to match a UID seen in /proc/<PID>/cgroup)
Restart a deployment's pods one by one
Go back to the deployment's previous version
Run N pods of a deployment (0 stops it)
No new pods on a node; running pods stay
Move a node's pods elsewhere before maintenance
Let pods be scheduled on the node again
Delete one pod; its deployment starts a new one

pitfalls: Check the cluster before any change: kubectl config current-context. Each cluster login is its own context.
Without -n, kubectl uses the current context's namespace (often default).
kubectl logs shows the running container; after a crash, add --previous.
kubectl drain stops at pods with local (emptyDir) data; --delete-emptydir-data deletes that data.
Logins through kubectl plugins (such as kubectl vsphere login) are not covered by la.
